segments.heading: Function `plan_part`: one kernel field of a plan line (trial mode)
segments.text:
- Trial mode only. The code of the trial mode starts at line 1795, in the rows above. The whole-chip test never calls this function. `main` does not enter the trial mode there (lines 2912 to 2914).
- It reads one field of a plan line into `*p`: the index of the kernel in `kernels[]`, the size in bytes and the duration in ms.
- With `with_ms` = 1 the field has the form `KERNEL@SIZE:MS`. The text `-` is also allowed. It means that this part is absent, and `p->k` stays -1. With `with_ms` = 0 the form is `KERNEL@SIZE`.
- Checks: the text is shorter than 96 characters, the name is in `kernels[]`, the kernel is a read kernel, the size is above 0, a multiple of 256 bytes and at most `--bytes`, the duration is 1 ms to 3600000 ms (1 hour).
- A defect goes to `plan_bad` (line 2554). It prints the plan path, the line number and a message to stderr and ends the process with status 2. `plan_size` and `plan_long` (lines 2566 to 2597) convert the numbers.

segments.heading: Function `plan_pairs`: line 2 of the plan file (trial mode)
segments.text:
- Trial mode only. The whole-chip test does not run it.
- Line 2 of the plan file has the form `# key=value key=value ...`. The function splits it at each space and keeps a pointer to every pair in `plan.pair`. At most 64 pairs are allowed.
- The pair `bytes=` must equal `--bytes`. The pair `cpu=` must equal the first CPU of `--cpus`. Both pairs must be present. Otherwise `plan_bad` ends the process.

segments.heading: Function `plan_trial`: one trial line of the plan (trial mode)
segments.text:
- Trial mode only. The whole-chip test does not run it.
- Lines 2668 to 2677 split one trial line at single spaces into exactly 11 fields. Their names stand in `PLAN_LINE3` (line 1816): trial, cond, rep, prev, pfx, pred, tgt, nwin, win_ms, count, bins.
- Lines 2678 to 2682 add one `struct trial` to the array `plan.tr` and keep the 11 field texts in it.
- Lines 2683 to 2688 check the trial number (0, 1, 2, ... in file order), `cond` (no comma) and `rep` (1 to 4).
- Lines 2689 to 2692: `plan_part` reads the four parts of the trial: previous activity (`prev`), prefix (`pfx`), predecessor (`pred`) and target (`tgt`). The first three may be `-`. The target has no duration field.

- Continues `plan_trial`. The duration of a prefix must be a multiple of 4 ms. `nwin` (the number of target windows) must be 1 to 4096. `win_ms` (the duration of one target window) must be 1 ms to 3600000 ms.
- `count` must be the word `closed`, `open` or `read`. `bins` must be 0 or 1.
- Lines 2707 to 2721 compute in `recsz` the storage that the records of all trials up to this line need: trial records, windows, bins, counter readings, trace events and the pad of `--rec-pad`. A total above 256 MiB (`MAX_REC_BYTES`) ends the process.

segments.heading: Function `read_plan`: reads and checks the whole plan (trial mode)
segments.text:
- Trial mode only. The whole-chip test does not run it.
- Reads the whole plan file (`plan.path`, the value of `--plan`) into memory. The text buffer starts with 65536 bytes and doubles when it is full. A file that cannot be read ends the process with status 2.
- Lines 2748 to 2750 compute a 64-bit checksum of the file bytes (the FNV-1a hash) into `plan.hash`.
- Lines 2751 to 2752 refuse a file that holds a zero byte.

- Continues `read_plan`. The loop goes through the text line by line.
- Line 1 must be the text `# bwx8-plan v1`. Line 3 must be the line of column names `PLAN_LINE3` (line 1816).
- Line 2 goes to `plan_pairs`. Every line from line 4 on is one trial and goes to `plan_trial`.
- A plan with fewer than 3 lines, or without a trial, ends the process through `plan_bad`.

segments.heading: Function `trial_usage`: option summary of the trial mode
segments.text: Trial mode only. Prints the option summary of the trial mode to stderr and ends the process with status 2. The whole-chip test does not reach it.

segments.heading: Function `trial_main`: entry of the trial mode (not run by the test)
segments.text:
- `main` calls this function only when an argument is the word `--trial` (lines 2912 to 2914). No argument line of the whole-chip test holds that word [Ref4]. So the test never runs it.
- Lines 2807 to 2847 are one loop over the arguments. Options of the trial mode only: `--trace`, `--hot-copy`, `--rec-pad`, `--evict-mb`, `--plan` and `--ctl-cpu`. Options that the interval mode also has: `--no-thp`, `--cpus`, `--bytes`, `--pmu-type` and `--events`.
- Any other argument goes to `trial_usage`, which ends the process. The options `--threads`, `--seq`, `--stop`, `--start`, `--rounds`, `--min-ms` and `--count` of the test have no branch in this loop.

- Continues `trial_main`. Checks: `--cpus` names exactly one CPU, `--bytes` is given and is a multiple of 256 bytes, `--plan` is given. The CPU of the controlling thread (`--ctl-cpu`, default 0) differs from the worker CPU. Both CPUs are in the allowed CPU set of the process.
- `read_plan` (line 2725) reads and checks the plan. When a trial of the plan counts events, the PMU type and the events must be known, from the options or from the environment variables BWX_PMU_TYPE and BWX_EVENTS.
- Lines 2878 to 2885: the controlling thread (the main thread of the trial mode) pins itself with `pin_cpu`. It starts one thread that runs `trial_worker` (line 2449), waits for its end and returns 0.

segments.heading: Include of the self-test file
segments.text: The include lines of the two older self-test files (bwx10_selftest.c and bwx11_selftest.c) stand between `#if 0` and `#endif`. So the compiler skips them. Line 2900 includes bwx12_selftest.c, which defines the function `selftest`. `main` calls it only for the option `--selftest` (line 2920), and no argument line of the whole-chip test holds this option [Ref4].

segments.heading: Function `main`: start of the program
segments.text: Entry point of the program. `threads_given` records that `--threads` was given. `seq_text` will hold a copy of the `--seq` text for header line 2 of the output.
Process start time: one reading of the clock CLOCK_MONOTONIC through `now_ns` (line 327), in ns. The T rows print the common start, `t0` and `t1` of each thread as seconds after this time.

`page_bytes` is the size of one small memory page, as Linux reports it. `alloc_buf` (line 434) uses it when it places a buffer inside its mapping. `cfg.bytes` gets its default of 1 MiB here. `--bytes 256M` replaces it at line 2937.

`restrict_cpus` (line 368) removes every CPU above 119 from the allowed CPU set of the process. The script rx.sh has already limited the process to the CPUs 0 to 119 with `taskset` [Ref3]. So this call changes nothing in the test.

segments.heading: `main`: mode choice, interval mode or trial mode
segments.text:
- The loop compares every argument with the word `--trial`. When one is equal, `main` returns the result of `trial_main`, and no line below runs.
- Line 2914 is the only call of `trial_main` in the file.
- The argument lines of like.spec, cfwd.spec and crev.spec do not hold the word `--trial` [Ref4]. So in the whole-chip test the loop ends without that call. The program continues in the interval mode, which is the rest of `main`.

segments.heading: `main`: argument parsing
segments.text: Loop over the arguments from left to right. `a` is the current argument. `more` is 1 when one more argument follows it. An option with a value is accepted only when `more` is 1, and `argv[++i]` then takes the value.
`--selftest` runs the self-test and ends the program. `--list` prints the 55 kernel names of `kernels[]` and ends the program. The argument lines of the test hold neither option [Ref4].

The argument lines of the test hold neither `--no-thp` nor `--two-buffers` [Ref4]. So `cfg.use_thp` keeps its default 1 (line 282), and `alloc_buf` asks Linux for 2 MiB pages. `cfg.two_buffers` stays 0 at this point.
`--count` (given in the test) sets `cfg.count` to 1. Then each worker opens its counter group and reads it before and after every timed interval. `main` prints the C rows from these readings.
`--threads 120`: `parse_long` (line 353) accepts a whole number from 1 to 4096. `cfg.threads` becomes 120.
`--cpus 0-63,64-119`: `parse_cpus` (line 388) appends the CPUs of each range to `cfg.cpus`, in the order of the text. The result is the list 0, 1, ... 119. `cfg.ncpus` becomes 120.
`--bytes 256M`: `parse_bytes` (line 334) reads the letter `M` as 2^20. `cfg.bytes` becomes 268435456 bytes (256 MiB). This is the buffer size of each thread.

`--min-ms 6000`: `strtod` reads the text as a decimal number of milliseconds. The number must be above 0 and at most 3.6e6 ms (1 hour). `cfg.min_s` becomes 6.0 s. With `--stop common` this is the time from the common start to the deadline (line 3061).
`--rounds 2`: a whole number from 1 to 1000000. `cfg.rounds` becomes 2. The program then runs the `--seq` list 2 times, as round 0 and round 1.

- `--seq`: line 2949 first copies the text to `seq_text`. `parse_seq` then splits the argument text itself at each comma.
- `parse_seq` (line 1750) looks up each name in `kernels[]` and appends its index to `cfg.seq`. An unknown name ends the process.
- Result: 5 entries for like.spec (`oldread`, `asmread`, `read_nop96`, `read_nop256`, `read_1pl`) and 3 entries for cfwd.spec and crev.spec [Ref4]. `cfg.nseq` holds this number.
- No name of the test has an `@SIZE` part. So the size of every entry stays 0 until line 2990.

`--stop common`: the value must be `pass` or `common`. Any other value goes to `usage`. `cfg.stop_common` becomes 1. Then all threads get one common start time and one common deadline for each interval (lines 3058 to 3063).
`--start common`: the value must be `common` or `offset`. `cfg.start_offset` becomes 0 for `common`. So every worker starts its timed loop at byte 0 of its own buffer (worker line 1662).

- `--pmu-type 11`: `cfg.pmu_type` becomes 11.
- `--events`: `parse_events` (line 1771) stores the 6 names in `cfg.ev_name` and the 6 codes in `cfg.ev_code`. `cfg.nev` becomes 6.
- `main` does not interpret the codes. Each worker passes them to Linux in `open_counters` (line 1582).

- Any other argument goes to `usage` (line 1737). The same holds for an option whose value is missing.
- `usage` prints the option summary to stderr and ends the process with status 2.
- Every option of the three argument lines of the test has a branch above [Ref4]. So the test does not reach these lines.

segments.heading: `main`: checks of the settings
segments.text: Two checks that end in `usage`. First: `--threads` needs `--cpus`. Second: the thread count, the round count and the number of `--seq` entries are at least 1, and `--bytes` is above 0 and a multiple of 256 bytes. The settings of the test pass both checks.

Fallback for the counter settings, for `--count` without `--pmu-type` or without `--events`. The program then takes the missing setting from the environment variable BWX_PMU_TYPE or BWX_EVENTS, if that variable is set. The argument lines of the test give both options [Ref4]. So these lines change nothing there.
With `--count` the PMU type and at least one event must be known at this point. Otherwise the program prints a message and ends through `usage`. In the test the type is 11 and there are 6 events.
Loop over the `--seq` entries. An entry without an `@SIZE` part gets the size of `--bytes`. In the test every entry gets 268435456 bytes.

- Size check of an entry. The size must be at most `--bytes` and a multiple of 256 bytes. Otherwise the program prints a message to stderr and ends through `usage`.
- With `--stop common` a size above 2 MiB (`CHUNK_BYTES`) must also be a multiple of 2 MiB. With this stop rule the worker calls the kernel on chunks of 2 MiB (worker line 1693).
- 268435456 bytes is 128 times 2 MiB. So the entries of the test pass.

A copy kernel in the list sets `cfg.two_buffers` to 1. The six kernels of the test have the type T_READ or T_OLDREAD in `kernels[]` (lines 1460 to 1476). So `cfg.two_buffers` stays 0, and each thread has one buffer, `a`. Header line 2 of every csv file of the test says `two_buffers=0` [Ref5].
A warning on stderr when there are more threads than CPUs in the list. The test has 120 threads and 120 CPUs. So no warning is printed.

segments.heading: `main`: thread records, barrier, start of the workers
segments.text:
- Three arrays, filled with 0 by `calloc`.
- `th`: one record per thread (120 in the test).
- `bufs`: two buffer addresses per thread, for buffer `a` and buffer `b` (240 entries).
- `pg`: one page-state record per entry of `bufs` (240 entries).
Creates the barrier `bar` for the thread count plus 1. In the test this is 121: the 120 workers and the main thread. A failed allocation or a failed barrier setup ends the program with status 2.

- Starts the workers. Thread `i` gets the index `i` and the CPU `cfg.cpus[i % cfg.ncpus]`.
- With 120 threads and the CPU list 0 to 119 this is CPU `i`. So threads 0 to 63 run on mesh 0 and threads 64 to 119 run on mesh 1.
- Each new thread runs `worker` (line 1632). It pins itself, opens its counters, maps its buffer and writes it. `main` does not wait for that here. It continues with the header.
- `main` never pins itself in the interval mode. It may run on any CPU of the allowed CPU set, the CPUs 0 to 119.
- A failed `pthread_create` ends the program with status 2.

segments.heading: `main`: header lines of the csv file
segments.text:
- Header line 1. It gives the meaning of GB, the formula of the rate in the I rows, and four settings.
- In the test the settings are `threads=120 bytes_per_thread=268435456 min_ms=6000 thp=madvise` in all 9 csv files [Ref5].
- `thp=madvise` only says that the program asked for 2 MiB pages. The P rows show what the buffers got.

- Header line 2: the `--seq` text, the rounds, the stop rule, the start rule, `two_buffers`, `count` and the build kind.
- `STANDIN` is 0 in the AArch64 build (line 492). So the build kind is printed as `kernels=aarch64`. Every csv file of the test has this text [Ref5].
- The line also says that round and position count from 0, and that the times are seconds since the process start.
Header lines 3 to 5: the column names of the I rows, the T rows and the P rows. Lines 3077 to 3085 print the I rows and the T rows. `print_p` (line 1570) prints the P rows.

Header line 6, only with `--count`: the column names of the C rows. After `cputime_ns` it lists the event names in the order of `--events`. The line ends with the PMU type and the event codes in hexadecimal. In the test this is `pmu_type=11 codes=0x198,0x199,0x19a,0x19b,0x19c,0x19` [Ref5].
Writes the header lines to the standard output now. In the test the standard output is the csv file. The script rx.sh redirects it there [Ref3].

segments.heading: `main`: loop over rounds and positions
segments.text:
- Two nested loops, as in `worker` (lines 1656 to 1657). `round` runs from 0 to 1 in the test.
- `pos` starts at -1, not at 0. Position -1 is one extra loop pass before the first interval. Each position from 0 up is one timed interval.
- The test has 10 intervals per process for like.spec and 6 for cfwd.spec and crev.spec.
- `main` and the 120 workers go through the same rounds and positions. At each barrier call below a thread waits until all 121 threads have arrived.
The loop pass with position -1 is skipped in every round after round 0, and in a process with one thread. So in the test it runs once, before the first interval.

- Position -1. `main` calls the barrier. The call returns when all 120 workers have mapped and written their buffers and wait at worker line 1652.
- Then `main` copies the buffer addresses of every thread into `bufs`: entry `2 * i` for buffer `a`, entry `2 * i + 1` for buffer `b`.
- Buffer `b` does not exist in the test. Its entries stay NULL.
- This loop pass continues with the page-state block at line 3105. That block prints the page state before the first interval.

segments.heading: `main`: one interval, common start
segments.text: One interval. `e` is the `--seq` entry of this position, and `name` is the name of its kernel. `per_pass` is the byte count of one pass over the buffer: 268435456 in the test (a copy kernel counts twice the size). `total` and `max_el` start at 0.

- First barrier call of the interval. It returns when all 120 workers have finished the warm-up pass of this kernel and wait at worker line 1675.
- The barrier then lets all 121 threads continue.
- With `--stop common` the workers do not start the kernel yet. Each worker spins until `gen` changes (worker line 1677).

- **Common start, set by the main thread.** `main` reads the clock once and adds `LEAD_NS` (2 ms, line 132). The result `sched` is the common start time of all threads.
- It stores `sched` in `t_sched_ns`. It stores the deadline in `deadline_ns`: `sched` plus `cfg.min_s`, which is 6 s (6000000000 ns) in the test.
- Only after both stores it adds 1 to `gen`. So a worker that sees the new `gen` reads the new start time and the new deadline.
- Each worker then spins on the clock until `sched` and reads its own start time `t0` (worker lines 1681 to 1688).
- After the change of `gen`, `main` passes nothing more to the workers. Each worker stops on its own, at its first clock read at or after the deadline (worker lines 1700 to 1701).
- `main` is not pinned. In the test it runs these lines on one of the CPUs 0 to 119, and a pinned worker spins on each of these CPUs at that time.

- Second barrier call of the interval. `main` calls it directly after the change of `gen`.
- `main` blocks here until all 120 workers have stored their results and wait at worker line 1727.
- So between the change of `gen` and the end of the timed interval this call is the only code that `main` runs. It prints nothing in that time.

segments.heading: `main`: I row, T rows, C rows
segments.text:
- Loop over the results of the 120 threads. `total` becomes the sum of their byte counts.
- `max_el` becomes the longest elapsed time of one thread, `t_end - t_start` in ns. `t_start` is the `t0` of the worker, and `t_end` is its last `t1` (worker lines 1722 to 1723).
- From here to line 3114 every worker waits at the barrier of worker line 1731. So no kernel runs while `main` prints the I, T and C rows.
Branch for a process with one thread. There the worker reads the page state itself before the interval, and `main` prints it here. The test has 120 threads. So these lines do not run.

- **I row**: one per interval, 9 fields: `I`, round, position, kernel name, `bytes_per_thread`, thread count, `total_bytes`, `max_elapsed_s`, `aggregate_GBps`.
- `bytes_per_thread` is the size of the `--seq` entry (268435456 bytes in the test). It is a setting, not a measured value.
- `max_elapsed_s` is `max_el` in seconds, with 6 decimals.
- `aggregate_GBps` is `total` in bytes divided by `max_el` in ns, with 2 decimals. One byte per ns is 1 GB/s with GB = 1e9 bytes. So this rate is the bytes of all threads divided by the longest time of one thread.
- The script stat_bwx.py computes the rate of an interval in another way: the sum over the T rows of bytes / elapsed seconds / 1e9, in GB/s. It keeps the I value next to it as `I_agg` [Ref6].
- In the 74 intervals of the 9 csv files of the test the two values differ by less than 0.004 % (computed on 2026-11-21) [Ref5].

- **T rows**: one per thread and interval, 13 fields. Fields 1 to 6: `T`, round, position, kernel name, thread index (`tid`), CPU of the thread.
- Field 7 `bytes`: the byte count of the worker. Field 8 `elapsed_s`: `t_end - t_start` in seconds, with 6 decimals.
- The rate of a thread is field 7 divided by field 8, in bytes per second. The program does not print it. The script stat_bwx.py computes it and divides it by 1e9 to get GB/s [Ref6].
- Fields 9 to 11 (`t_sched_s`, `t_start_s`, `t_end_s`): the common start time, `t0` and the last `t1`, in seconds since the process start `t_base_ns`.
- Field 12 `passes`: `bytes / per_pass`, the number of passes over the buffer, with 3 decimals. Field 13 `flags`: `late` when `t0` came more than 100 us after the common start (worker line 1725), otherwise `-`.
- In the 9 csv files of the test no T row is `late`. The largest `t_start_s - t_sched_s` is 34 us (0.034 ms, computed on 2026-11-21) [Ref5].
**C rows**, only with `--count`: one per thread and interval. The first 6 fields are `C`, round, position, kernel name, thread index and CPU.

- Fields 7 and 8, `enabled_ns` and `running_ns`: the enabled time and the running time of the counter group at the second reading minus the same values at the first reading. A thread without an open group gets `NA,NA`.
- Field 9, `cputime_ns`: the thread CPU time at the second reading minus the value at the first reading.
- The worker takes the first reading (`c0`) directly before `t0` and the second reading (`c1`) directly after its last `t1` (worker lines 1684 to 1687 and 1717 to 1720).

One field per event, in the order of `--events`: the count at the second reading minus the count at the first reading. `ev_pos[ev]` is the place of the event in the group reading. It is -1 when the event did not open, and then the field is `NA`. In the 9 csv files of the test no field is `NA` [Ref5].

segments.heading: `main`: page state, P rows, `# page_read` line
segments.text:
- Page-state block. It runs in a process with more than one thread: once at position -1 and once after every interval.
- At this time every worker waits at a barrier: worker line 1653 after position -1, worker line 1731 after an interval. So no kernel runs while `main` reads the page state.
- `vm` will hold the four vmstat counters.

`main` reads the clock, reads the page state and reads the clock again. `read_smaps` (line 1515) looks up each of the 240 entries of `bufs` in `/proc/self/smaps` and skips the NULL entries. `read_vmstat` (line 1545) reads the four vmstat counters. `ms` is the duration of both readings in ms.
Barrier call that lets the workers continue. Each worker then starts the warm-up pass of the next interval, while `main` prints the P rows below. After the last interval the workers end instead.

- **P rows**: one per existing buffer, printed by `print_p` (line 1570). Entry `i` of `bufs` belongs to thread `i / 2`. An even `i` is buffer `a`.
- Fields: `P`, round, position, thread index, buffer letter, size of the buffer in kB, part on 2 MiB pages in kB, then the four vmstat counters.
- The position is that of the interval before the reading, or -1 for the reading before the first interval.
- All rows of one block carry the same four vmstat values. They count for the whole system and were read once (line 3112).
- In the test every P row is a row of buffer `a` and reports 262144 kB of 262144 kB on 2 MiB pages [Ref5].

The line `# page_read,round,pos,<time> ms`: the duration `ms` of the page-state reading of this block, with 3 decimals. In the 9 csv files of the test it lies between 3.745 ms and 4.947 ms (83 lines, read on 2026-11-21) [Ref5].

- Writes all rows that are still in the output buffer to the csv file. Then the loops continue with the next position.
- A new timed interval cannot start before `main` has passed line 3057 and line 3062 again. So `main` writes no output during a timed interval.
- Measured in the test: the time from the latest `t_end_s` of one interval to the `t_sched_s` of the next interval of the same process. It is 63.8 ms to 139.8 ms (65 pairs in the 9 csv files, computed on 2026-11-21) [Ref5].
- In this time lie the output of the rows, the page-state reading, the barrier calls, the warm-up pass of the next kernel and the 2 ms lead. No code of the interval mode calls a sleep function.

segments.heading: `main`: end
segments.text: After the last interval `main` waits for the end of all 120 worker threads. Then the process ends with status 0. The script rx.sh writes this status to the file launches.txt of the result folder [Ref3].
